request.user:
[2024 summer phd probability — problem 4]

Part II. Let $(V, E)$ be a finite undirected graph, $V = \{1, \dots, n\}$, with $v \sim v'$ iff $\{v, v'\} \in E$. State space $\mathcal{X} = \{-1, 1\}^n$ (spin configurations). Define $H(x) = \sum_{\{v,v'\}\in E}\mathbb{1}\{x(v) \ne x(v')\} = \tfrac12\sum_{\{v,v'\}\in E}(1 - x(v)x(v'))$ and $\pi(x) = \frac{e^{-H(x)}}{\sum_y e^{-H(y)}}$. The update $X_{t+1} = f_{t+1}(x_t)$: sample $v_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}(V)$, $S_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}\{-1,1\}$, $U_{t+1} \sim \mathrm{Unif}[0,1]$; propose $y$ with $y(v_{t+1}) = S_{t+1}$, $y(w) = x_t(w)$ otherwise; accept ($f_{t+1}(x_t) = y$) if $U_{t+1} \le \min\{1, e^{-H(y)}/e^{-H(x_t)}\}$, else reject. $P(x, z) = P(f_{t+1}(x) = z)$.
(1) Compute $P(x, z)$ for $z \ne x$ with $P(x, z) > 0$ (need not compute $P(x, x)$).
(2) Prove $\pi$ is stationary for this chain.
(3) With $N_{t+1} \subset V$ the neighbors of $v_{t+1}$ and $y$ the proposed move, show $\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x_t)}} = \exp(\tfrac12\sum_{w \in N_{t+1}}(S_{t+1} - x_t(v_{t+1})) x_t(w))$.
(4) Write $x \preceq y$ if $x(v) \le y(v)$ for all $v$. Prove that if $x \preceq z$ then $P(f_{t+1}(x) \preceq f_{t+1}(z)) = 1$ (handle $S_{t+1} = \pm1$ separately) — i.e. the dynamics is monotone.
(5) Let $\underline x = (-1, \dots, -1)$, $\bar x = (1, \dots, 1)$. Prove $F = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1$ is constant iff $F(\underline x) = F(\bar x)$. Let $T = \min\{t \ge 1 : f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\underline x) = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\bar x)\}$.
(6) For $z \in \mathcal{X}$, let $h(z)$ be the max number $k$ of distinct states $x_1 \preceq \cdots \preceq x_k = z$. Prove that if $x_t \preceq y_t$ and $x_t \ne y_t$ then $h(x_t) + 1 \le h(y_t)$.
(7) With $X_t = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\underline x)$, $Y_t = f_t \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\bar x)$ (so $\{T > t\} = \{X_t \ne Y_t\}$), prove $P(T > t) \le \mathbb{E}[h(Y_t) - h(X_t)]$.
(8) Prove $0 \le h(z) \le |V|$ and $\mathbb{E}[h(Y_t) - h(X_t)] \le |V|\,\bar d(t)$.
(9) If $|V| = 2L$ ($L > 1$ integer) and $k \ge 0$, prove $P(T > t_{\mathrm{mix}}(k + L)) \le \frac{1}{2^k}$ (state the properties of $d, \bar d, t_{\mathrm{mix}}$ used).
(10) Prove $\mathbb{E}[T] \le c\, L\, t_{\mathrm{mix}}$ for an absolute constant $c > 0$ (you may first show any nonnegative $U$ with $P(U > k) \le 1/2^k$ for all integers $k \ge 0$ has finite expectation).

response.text:
Let \(n=|V|\). Write \(x(v)\) also as \(x_v\). For \(x,z\in\mathcal X\), let  
\[
\Delta(x,z):=\{v\in V:x(v)\neq z(v)\}.
\]

## (1) Transition probabilities \(P(x,z)\) for \(z\neq x\)

A nontrivial move changes at most one coordinate. Hence \(P(x,z)>0\) for \(z\neq x\) iff \(|\Delta(x,z)|=1\). If \(\Delta(x,z)=\{v\}\), then necessarily \(z(v)=-x(v)\), and the proposal \(z\) is made exactly when \(v_{t+1}=v\) and \(S_{t+1}=z(v)\), which has probability \(1/(2n)\). Therefore
\[
P(x,z)
=
\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\frac1{2n}\min\{1,e^{H(x)-H(z)}\}.
\]
If \(|\Delta(x,z)|\neq 1\), then \(P(x,z)=0\) for \(z\neq x\).

---

## (2) Stationarity of \(\pi\)

We prove detailed balance. Let
\[
Z=\sum_{y\in\mathcal X} e^{-H(y)}.
\]
If \(x\neq z\) and \(|\Delta(x,z)|=1\), then by part (1),
\[
P(x,z)=\frac1{2n}\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)
=
\frac{e^{-H(x)}}{Z}\cdot \frac1{2n}
\min\left\{1,\frac{e^{-H(z)}}{e^{-H(x)}}\right\}
=
\frac1{2nZ}\min\{e^{-H(x)},e^{-H(z)}\}.
\]
The right-hand side is symmetric in \(x,z\). Hence
\[
\pi(x)P(x,z)=\pi(z)P(z,x).
\]
If \(x,z\) differ in more than one coordinate, then both transition probabilities are \(0\). The diagonal case is trivial. Therefore \(P\) is reversible with respect to \(\pi\). By detailed balance, \(\pi\) is stationary.

---

## (3) Local form of the acceptance ratio

Let \(v=v_{t+1}\), \(S=S_{t+1}\), and \(N=N_{t+1}\) be the neighbors of \(v\). Let \(x=x_t\), and let \(y\) be the proposed configuration, so \(y(v)=S\) and \(y(w)=x(w)\) for \(w\neq v\).

Only edges incident to \(v\) can change their contribution to \(H\). For an edge \(\{v,w\}\),
\[
\frac12(1-y(v)y(w))-\frac12(1-x(v)x(w))
=
\frac12(1-Sx(w))-\frac12(1-x(v)x(w))
=
\frac12(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]
Therefore
\[
H(y)-H(x)
=
\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(x(v)-S)x(w).
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{e^{-H(y)}}{e^{-H(x)}}
=
\exp\{-(H(y)-H(x))\}
=
\exp\left(\frac12\sum_{w\in N}(S-x(v))x(w)\right).
\]

---

## (4) Monotonicity of the update map

We couple two chains using the same randomness \((v,S,U)\). Suppose \(x\preceq z\). We prove
\[
f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)
\]
for every realization of \((v,S,U)\).

Coordinates other than \(v\) are unchanged, so the order can only fail at coordinate \(v\).

### Case 1: \(S=+1\)

If \(z(v)=+1\), then the upper chain has spin \(+1\) at \(v\) after the update, so the lower spin is automatically \(\leq +1\).

The only nontrivial case is \(z(v)=-1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), this forces \(x(v)=z(v)=-1\). By part (3), the acceptance ratios are
\[
R_x=\exp\left(\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right),
\qquad
R_z=\exp\left(\sum_{w\sim v}z(w)\right).
\]
Since \(x(w)\le z(w)\) for every \(w\),
\[
\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\le \sum_{w\sim v}z(w),
\]
so \(R_x\le R_z\), and therefore
\[
\min\{1,R_x\}\le \min\{1,R_z\}.
\]
Thus if the lower chain accepts the move to \(+1\), then the upper chain also accepts. Hence order is preserved.

### Case 2: \(S=-1\)

If \(x(v)=-1\), then the lower chain has spin \(-1\) at \(v\) after the update, so it remains \(\leq\) the upper spin.

The only nontrivial case is \(x(v)=+1\). Since \(x\preceq z\), this forces \(x(v)=z(v)=+1\). The acceptance ratios are
\[
R_x=\exp\left(-\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\right),
\qquad
R_z=\exp\left(-\sum_{w\sim v}z(w)\right).
\]
Again \(x(w)\le z(w)\), so
\[
-\sum_{w\sim v}x(w)\ge -\sum_{w\sim v}z(w),
\]
and hence \(R_x\ge R_z\). Therefore
\[
\min\{1,R_x\}\ge \min\{1,R_z\}.
\]
Thus if the upper chain accepts the move to \(-1\), then the lower chain also accepts. Hence order is preserved.

Therefore
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(f_{t+1}(x)\preceq f_{t+1}(z)\bigr)=1.
\]

---

## (5) Constant maps and coalescence of top and bottom

Let
\[
\underline x=(-1,\dots,-1),\qquad \bar x=(1,\dots,1).
\]
By part (4), each update map \(f_i\) is monotone, and therefore the composition
\[
F=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1
\]
is monotone.

If \(F\) is constant, then clearly
\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]

Conversely, suppose
\[
F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]
For any \(x\in\mathcal X\),
\[
\underline x\preceq x\preceq \bar x.
\]
By monotonicity of \(F\),
\[
F(\underline x)\preceq F(x)\preceq F(\bar x).
\]
Since the two endpoints are equal, this forces
\[
F(x)=F(\underline x)=F(\bar x).
\]
Thus \(F\) is constant.

Therefore \(F\) is constant iff \(F(\underline x)=F(\bar x)\).

---

## (6) The height function

There is a harmless off-by-one issue in the statement: if \(h(z)\) literally counts the number of states in a chain ending at \(z\), then \(h(\bar x)=n+1\), contradicting part (8). The intended height is the number of strict steps in the longest chain:
\[
h(z):=\max\{k:\ x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_k=z\},
\]
where \(x\prec y\) means \(x\preceq y\) and \(x\neq y\).

With this convention, if \(x_t\preceq y_t\) and \(x_t\neq y_t\), take a longest strict chain ending at \(x_t\):
\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t.
\]
Since \(x_t\prec y_t\), appending \(y_t\) gives a strict chain
\[
x_0\prec x_1\prec\cdots\prec x_{h(x_t)}=x_t\prec y_t.
\]
Hence
\[
h(y_t)\ge h(x_t)+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
h(x_t)+1\le h(y_t).
\]

---

## (7) Bounding \(\mathbb P(T>t)\)

Let
\[
X_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\underline x),
\qquad
Y_t=f_t\circ\cdots\circ f_1(\bar x).
\]
By monotonicity,
\[
X_t\preceq Y_t
\]
for every \(t\). Also,
\[
\{T>t\}=\{X_t\neq Y_t\}.
\]
On the event \(\{X_t\neq Y_t\}\), part (6) gives
\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)\ge 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbf 1_{\{T>t\}}\le h(Y_t)-h(X_t).
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\mathbb P(T>t)
\le
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)].
\]

---

## (8) Bounds on \(h\) and on its expected gap

For \(z\in\mathcal X\), let
\[
m(z):=\#\{v\in V:z(v)=+1\}.
\]
In the coordinatewise partial order, every strict step in a chain must change at least one coordinate from \(-1\) to \(+1\). Therefore no chain ending at \(z\) can have more than \(m(z)\) strict steps. Conversely, starting from \(\underline x\), we can flip the \(+1\)-coordinates of \(z\) one at a time, obtaining a strict chain of length \(m(z)\). Hence
\[
h(z)=m(z).
\]
Thus
\[
0\le h(z)\le |V|.
\]

Now let \(\mu_t\) be the law of \(X_t\) and \(\nu_t\) the law of \(Y_t\). Then
\[
\mu_t=P^t(\underline x,\cdot),
\qquad
\nu_t=P^t(\bar x,\cdot).
\]
Because \(X_t\preceq Y_t\),
\[
h(Y_t)-h(X_t)
=
\sum_{v\in V}\bigl(\mathbf 1\{Y_t(v)=+1\}-\mathbf 1\{X_t(v)=+1\}\bigr).
\]
Taking expectations,
\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\sum_{v\in V}\left(\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)\right),
\]
where
\[
A_v:=\{z\in\mathcal X:z(v)=+1\}.
\]
For each \(v\),
\[
|\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)|
\le
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le
\bar d(t),
\]
where
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
\le
|V|\,\bar d(t).
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of the mixing time

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Use the standard definitions
\[
d(t):=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
and
\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard properties:

1. Triangle inequality:
   \[
   \bar d(t)\le 2d(t).
   \]

2. Submultiplicativity of \(\bar d\):
   \[
   \bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t).
   \]

Let \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(d(\tau)\le 1/4\),
\[
\bar d(\tau)\le 2d(\tau)\le \frac12.
\]
By submultiplicativity,
\[
\bar d(m\tau)\le \left(\frac12\right)^m.
\]
Using parts (7) and (8),
\[
\mathbb P(T>m\tau)
\le
|V|\,\bar d(m\tau)
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-m}.
\]
Take \(m=k+L\). Then
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
=
\frac{2L}{2^L}\cdot 2^{-k}.
\]
Since \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Let again \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(T\) is integer-valued,
\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\sum_{s=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>s).
\]
Partition the sum into blocks of length \(\tau\):
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau).
\]
Split the sum at \(j=L\):
\[
\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau)
=
\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\mathbb P(T>j\tau)
+
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>(L+k)\tau).
\]
The first sum is at most \(L\). By part (9), the second sum is at most
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}=2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau(L+2).
\]
Since \(L>1\), \(L+2\le 2L\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.}
\]
Thus the desired bound holds with an absolute constant, for example \(c=2\).

\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
=
\sum_{v\in V}\left(\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)\right),
\]
where
\[
A_v:=\{z\in\mathcal X:z(v)=+1\}.
\]
For each \(v\),
\[
|\nu_t(A_v)-\mu_t(A_v)|
\le
\|\nu_t-\mu_t\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le
\bar d(t),
\]
where
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\mathbb E[h(Y_t)-h(X_t)]
\le
|V|\,\bar d(t).
\]

---

## (9) Tail bound at multiples of the mixing time

Assume \(|V|=2L\), with \(L>1\).

Use the standard definitions
\[
d(t):=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
\[
\bar d(t):=\max_{x,y\in\mathcal X}\|P^t(x,\cdot)-P^t(y,\cdot)\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\]
and
\[
t_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\min\{t:d(t)\le 1/4\}.
\]

We use the standard properties:

1. Triangle inequality:
   \[
   \bar d(t)\le 2d(t).
   \]

2. Submultiplicativity of \(\bar d\):
   \[
   \bar d(s+t)\le \bar d(s)\bar d(t).
   \]

Let \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(d(\tau)\le 1/4\),
\[
\bar d(\tau)\le 2d(\tau)\le \frac12.
\]
By submultiplicativity,
\[
\bar d(m\tau)\le \left(\frac12\right)^m.
\]
Using parts (7) and (8),
\[
\mathbb P(T>m\tau)
\le
|V|\,\bar d(m\tau)
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-m}.
\]
Take \(m=k+L\). Then
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2L\cdot 2^{-(k+L)}
=
\frac{2L}{2^L}\cdot 2^{-k}.
\]
Since \(L>1\), we have \(2L\le 2^L\). Therefore
\[
\mathbb P(T>(k+L)t_{\mathrm{mix}})
\le
2^{-k}.
\]

---

## (10) Bound on \(\mathbb E[T]\)

Let again \(\tau=t_{\mathrm{mix}}\). Since \(T\) is integer-valued,
\[
\mathbb E[T]
=
\sum_{s=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>s).
\]
Partition the sum into blocks of length \(\tau\):
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau).
\]
Split the sum at \(j=L\):
\[
\sum_{j=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>j\tau)
=
\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}\mathbb P(T>j\tau)
+
\sum_{k=0}^\infty \mathbb P(T>(L+k)\tau).
\]
The first sum is at most \(L\). By part (9), the second sum is at most
\[
\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{-k}=2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[T]
\le
\tau(L+2).
\]
Since \(L>1\), \(L+2\le 2L\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[T]\le 2L\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}.}
\]
Thus the desired bound holds with an absolute constant, for example \(c=2\).
